Discussion
We explain the microscopic origin of magnon lifetime inversion through mode-dependent damping torques. Figure 4d and e schematically illustrate the FMR and EXR modes, respectively, for \delta s < 0 and \alpha TM \ll \alpha RE so that \alpha s- < 0. These figures show how the two damping torques, sgn(\delta s) \alpha s+ n \times n_ (green arrow) and sgn(\delta s) \alpha s- 2 s / \rho n \times (n€ \times n) (red arrow), act differently depending on the resonance mode. The coefficient sgn(\delta s) implies these damping torques are inverted depending on the sign of the net spin density. The black arrows represent the effective field of each mode, whereas the gray arrow represents n.

In Fig. 4d, the dominant effective field inducing the FMR mode arises from the PMA energy density. As a result, n precesses around the PMA field, Heff,FMR. Considering the time derivatives of n, both sgn(\delta s) \alpha s+ n \times n_ and sgn(\delta s) \alpha s- 2 s / \rho n \times (n€ \times n) point to the same direction, acting as damping torques in the FMR mode. In contrast, in Fig. 4e, the effective field generating the EXR mode arises from the exchange energy. Consequently, n processes around the exchange field Heff,EXR, which is proportional to -\rho n€. Similar to the FMR mode, sgn(\delta s) \alpha s+ n \times n_ acts as a damping torque. However, sgn(\delta s) \alpha s- 2 s / \rho n \times (n€ \times n) now points in the opposite direction to sgn(\delta s) \alpha s+ n \times n_, effectively functioning as an anti-damping torque. Therefore, sgn(\delta s) \alpha s- 2 s / \rho n \times (n€ \times n) serves as a mode-dependent damping torque, providing the microscopic origin for magnon lifetime inversion.

The EXR mode frequency scales with the square root of the product of the anisotropy and exchange fields, while the FMR mode frequency depends only on the anisotropy field. Since the exchange field is generally much stronger, the EXR mode frequency is much higher, making it attractive for ferrimagnetic spintronics11. However, the magnon lifetime (\tau) of the FMR mode scales inversely with the anisotropy field, whereas that of the EXR mode scales inversely with the exchange field. Consequently, when both sublattices have equal damping constants, the EXR mode exhibits a shorter magnon lifetime than the FMR mode due to its higher frequency. Our study, however, reveals that when the damping constants of the two sublattices differ substantially, the EXR mode can exhibit a longer magnon lifetime than the FMR mode near the angular momentum compensation condition, thereby overcoming this limitation. This finding suggests that engineering sublattice-specific damping offers a promising strategy to achieve both high frequency and extended magnon lifetime in the EXR mode. The combination of higher frequency and longer magnon lifetime of the EXR mode could also result in substantially lower effective damping compared to the FMR mode (Fig. 3e), further enhancing the viability of the EXR mode for future spintronic applications, such as the sub-THz oscillators40,41 and circuits42.

## Methods

Sample fabrication and characterization
We deposited film stacks of Ta(1nm)/Pt(6nm)/Co1−xGdx(7nm)/TaOx(2nm) films onto oxidized Si substrates via magnetron sputtering at room temperature with a base pressure below 5 × 10−8 torr (ATC, AJA International). The Co1−xGdx layer was grown by Co and Gd co-sputtering, with Co sputtering power fixed at 120 W and Gd sputtering power varied from 40 to 120 W to achieve different Gd concentrations. The Ta layers at the bottom and top enhance adhesion and prevent oxidation, respectively. The composition of Co1−xGdx was analyzed using energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (EDX). The hysteresis loops of the films were characterized using Kerr microscopy (TTT-02-Kerr Microscope, TuoTuo Technology). Vibrating sample magnetometry (VSM) measurements were conducted over a temperature range of 60–300 K using a physical property measurement system equipped with a VSM option (DynaCool, Quantum Design).

Time-resolved magneto-optical Kerr measurements
The laser source was an 80 MHz Ti:sapphire femtosecond oscillator (Mai Tai BB, Spectra-Physics) emitting pulses centered at 800 nm with a pulse duration < 80 fs. The original laser pulse was split into a pump and a probe pulse by a beam splitter. The pump pulse was then focused onto a \beta-barium borate (BBO) crystal to convert it to 400 nm, while the probe pulse was directed onto the sample after passing through a mechanical delay stage to control the optical path difference. Both pump and probe pulses were linearly polarized and focused onto the sample surface at normal incidence using a 50× objective lens, which formed a polar MOKE configuration. The typical fluences of the pump and probe pulses were 2 and 0.9 mJ cm−2, respectively. The sample was placed in an optical cryostat (Cryostation S50, Montana Instruments) for magnetic-field-dependent and temperature-dependent measurements.

Numerical simulations
We carried out numerical simulations based on the Landau–Lifshitz–Gilbert (LLG) equation for a two-spin system, m_i = -\gamma i m i \times Heff,i + \alpha i m i \times m_i, where Heff,i = H + Hk m z,i z^ - Hex,i m j + H m \times D (i = TM, RE, j = RE, TM), Hk = K / (1/2 Ms,TM + Ms,RE), Hex,i = 2Aex / Ms,i d2, HD,TM = D / Ms,TM, HD,RE = -D / Ms,RE, and D = y^. \gamma i = gi \mu B / \hbar is the gyromagnetic ratio, gi is the Landé g factor, \alpha i is the damping parameter, K0 = K/4 is the PMA energy density of each sublattice, Aex is the exchange stiffness, d is the lattice constant, Ms,i is the saturation magnetization, and D is the DMI constant.
